title: Esteban Gonzalez
text:
In this lab, the STM32L432KC was used to read an array of frequency and duration numbers and generates a corresponding square wave to play a song on a speaker.



The design was developed using TIM15 and TIM16 for the duration and frequency. Additionally, my own device drivers were made from scratch using only the reference manual as a reference. A total of five header files were created to meet the design requirements.
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository



The minimum duration of a note was calculated the following way:
\(min = 80MHz / (80)(1000) = 1000 Hz = 1ms\)
The maximum duration of a note was calculated the following way:
\(max = uint32 ms = 4,294,967,295 ms = 49.71 days\)
The maximum frequency of a note was calculated the following way:
\(max = 80MHz / (1)(2) = 40 MHz\)
In reality, the human ear can’t hear such a high frequency and there is limitations to hardware that make the maximum frequency lower.
The minimum frequency was calculated the following way:
\(min = 80MHz / (65536)(65536) = 0.0186 Hz\)
The calculations for all the notes of Fur Elise is below:



Calculations


Checking just 220 Hz and 1000 Hz is not enough to gaurantee all the notes of Fur Elise fall within 1% error. This is because the notes could be noninteger values, which would lead to some errors due to rounding.






Schematic


The schematic in Figure 2 demonstrates the physical layout of the design. The pin was connected to a potentiameter. This allowed the volume of the speaker to be adjusted. The aplifier had a gain of 20, and allowed the music notes to be played at a suitable noise level.



All the prescribed tasks were accomplished successfully. The speaker played Fur Elise, and the code is able to be easily modified to play a song of the user’s choice. For my purpose, I played the Imperial March from Star Wars.



The LLM can be a useful tool to sift through large documents. When tasked to find a timer that is suitable for this project, it listed all the potential timers I can use. This list was the most helpful, as it narrows down the scope and allows you to easily go find those specific timers in the manual. It then made a suggestion to use TIM2. I did not use this timer, but it could be feasible using it.
It did say that it recommended the timer I used, which leads me to beleive it’s other suggestions are good as well. Over all, an LLM can be a useful tool to help narrow the scope down when lookng at a document. Instead of looking through a 1600 pages, it tells you what is feasible and where you can find more information on them. Much more manageable.

title: Smart High-CADR Air Purifier
text:
During the Summer of 2026, I conducted research with LILAQ at Harvey Mudd College, an organization that investigates local air quality in Claremont with a focus on air quality communication and interventions.
My work focused on interventions addressing indoor particulate matter (PM). PM is a type of air pollution consisting of microscopic particles ranging from 10 μm to 0.1 μm. Prolonged exposure allows these particles to deposit deep into lung tissues, causing severe health effects. In Southern California, the biggest summer sources of PM2.5 are fireworks and wildfires.
While people assume staying indoors protects them, porous building envelopes, open windows, HVAC policies, and indoor cooking can release hazardous levels of PM2.5 into living spaces. A cost-effective way to address this is the Corsi-Rosenthal (CR) box. Invented during the COVID-19 pandemic, standard CR boxes are accessible but often loud and bulky. To address these downsides, I engineered a new CR box replacing the standard box fan with PC fans, resulting in a unit that is significantly quieter and slimmer.
Research Question: How effective is a PC fan CR box air filter at reducing indoor PM2.5 related to wildfires, fireworks, and summertime smog in LA?

title: Smart High-CADR Air Purifier
text:
Background
The EPA sets 35 µg/m³ as the limit for safe exposure to PM2.5. A common issue with standard weather apps reporting the Air Quality Index (AQI) is that they report on a 12-hour average. Your phone might indicate the air is healthy when there are actually severe, localized spikes in pollution. Furthermore, many apps rely on algorithms rather than hyperlocal sensor data.
Monitoring hyperlocal air quality is crucial for public health. Accurate data allows the community to make informed decisions, aligning with LILAQ’s goal of increasing air quality literacy.

title: Smart High-CADR Air Purifier
text:
Methodology
The CR boxes were tested over three phases, starting with characterizing the performance of each individual unit inside Drinkward residence rooms. These rooms provided optimal insulation to ensure the building’s HVAC system wouldn’t significantly skew the PM decay rates.
To simulate pollution, incense was lit for 1-2 minutes, raising PM levels to roughly 200 µg/m³ (simulating standard indoor cooking levels). PurpleAir sensors recorded the PM levels in the room and the hallway. Once the filter was turned on, the PM decay data was graphed and calculated to find the Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR):
\[ CADR = ACH \times V \] (Where ACH is the air exchange per hour calculated from the decay lifetime \(\tau\), and \(V\) is the volume of the room).

Holiday Deployment
After characterization, the filters were deployed on the 4th of July across McGregor, Sprague, Olin, and Drinkward. Each location paired a filter-equipped room against a control room. The filters operated on a cycle (1 hour on, 2 hours off) to allow outside polluted air in, measuring the units’ ability to rapidly clear real-world holiday pollution.

title: Smart High-CADR Air Purifier
text:
Results & Discussion
Testing demonstrated that the DIY PC-fan air filters are highly effective, successfully addressing indoor air quality related to wildfires, fireworks, and summertime smog.
Build precision (specifically duct-taping the seals) played a minor role in efficiency, but even the worst-performing units easily purified small rooms. The 5-fan unit was 46% to 58% more effective than the 3-fan units. Overall, these DIY models matched the performance of commercial options while running drastically quieter.
The units are inexpensive and take approximately 5 hours to build (with 4.5 hours dedicated passively to 3D printing components).

Future Work
Future initiatives include collaborating with the makerspace to host workshops for the 7C community and publishing open-source templates. By sourcing recycled fans from campus departments, we can further drive down the unit cost. LILAQ is also developing a comprehensive dashboard to integrate this sensor data, providing actionable air quality suggestions to the local community.

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
This paper presents the design, deployment, and results of an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) used to map the underwater topography of Dana Point Harbor and characterize the temperature-depth relationship of the water body. The AUV was equipped with a sonar sensor consisting of a speaker and microphone for depth measurement, a thermistor for temperature sensing, and a pressure sensor for depth navigation.
The AUV was deployed at two sites: pHake Lake for initial testing and Dana Point Harbor for final data collection. Despite issues with GPS module accuracy, the team successfully post-processed sonar data to reconstruct accurate harbor floor depth profiles. Measured floor depths were consistent with published harbor survey data from the Dana Point Harbor Authority, with an error of about 0.1 m across the mapped area. The AUV dived to a depth of 3 meters, confirming that temperature decreases with depth (the lowest recorded temperature of 18.3°C closely matched our control thermometer at 18.15°C).

title: Autonomous Underwater Robot
text:
Introduction
Understanding the underwater topography and thermal structure of coastal environments is essential for a wide range of oceanographic applications. Ocean currents—which are influenced by temperature gradients and seafloor geometry—play a fundamental role in heat transport, nutrient cycling, and the distribution of marine species [1].
As ocean temperatures rise due to anthropogenic climate change, the thermal stratification of coastal waters is intensifying. This has direct consequences for dissolved oxygen levels, marine biodiversity, and the overall health of reef ecosystems [2]. Accurate, high-resolution measurements of temperature and depth are therefore critical for monitoring these changes and informing conservation efforts.

Project Goals

Topographical Mapping: Map the underwater topography of Dana Point Harbor using acoustic time-of-flight sonar to produce a depth profile of the harbor floor.
Thermal Profiling: Characterize the temperature-depth relationship within the water column, quantifying any thermal stratification present at the deployment site.

These measurements were carried out using a custom-built AUV capable of autonomous diving and surface navigation. The AUV was equipped with three primary sensors: a sonar transceiver for acoustic range finding, a thermistor circuit for water temperature measurement, and a pressure sensor.

title: CRPA Antenna Characterization
text:
Every aircraft in the sky relies on the Global Positioning System (GPS) to know its location. However, the signals which GPS satellites transmit are extremely weak and are susceptible to various forms of interference. On behalf of the FAA and Aerospace Corporation, our team is characterizing a new type of GPS antenna.


The Global Positioning System is an essential part of our world today. Data from GPS timing dictates financial markets, power grids, and transit. In civil aviation, GPS supports precision approaches and system navigation, so it is a nontrivial ordeal when these services go offline.
Reports of GPS interference affecting commercial aircraft have risen sharply over recent years. New conflicts across the globe have also accelerated GPS interference technology, mainly in the form of jamming. A jamming attack consists of transmitting radio-frequency energy at GPS frequencies, overpowering the extremely weak satellite signals.
Airplanes currently use Fixed Reception Pattern Antennas (FRPAs), which receive signals from the entire spatial spectrum. Controlled Reception Pattern Antennas (CRPAs) use an array of elements whose signal can be combined to place nulls in the direction of interference. The CRPA recently had its ITAR restriction taken away, so the door is now open to use CRPAs for civil aviation.
Manufacturers, regulators, and airlines need trustworthy performance data to evaluate CRPAs and their potential implementation. Commercially available datasheets often omit the testing conditions behind their published numbers. By creating a process to produce this data and document how we conduct measurements, we aim to fill this gap. The purpose of this study is to encourage the spread of CRPAs into civil aviation. In the long run, wider CRPA adoption would make civil aircraft significantly more resilient to jamming attacks.



Characterizing a GPS antenna means we have to measure its gain as a function of elevation and azimuth, its polarization purity, and its phase response. For a multi-element antenna like a CRPA, we must measure its elements individually. These quantities determine how well an antenna can reject interference.
Beginning with a single-element FRPA, these antennas are well documented, so comparing our measurements against known results lets us validate the test setup.

title: CRPA Antenna Characterization
text:
Background

Purpose and Scope
To understand the methodologies used to characterize the antennas provided by The Aerospace Corporation and the FAA, it is necessary to establish an understanding of antenna radiation, GPS signal characteristics, and radio frequency measurement techniques.


Antenna Fundamentals
An antenna’s performance is defined by how it directs and receives electromagnetic energy in three-dimensional space. The radiation pattern illustrates this directionality, with gain representing the antenna’s efficiency and directional focus. Key metrics include directivity, which measures how concentrated the beam is, and beamwidth, which defines the angular span of the primary signal.
Signal polarization describes the orientation of the electromagnetic wave’s field. Understanding the boundary between the near-field and far-field is important for accurate measurements, as true radiation patterns only stabilize in the far-field (\(d \ge \frac{2D^2}{\lambda}\)). In more advanced setups, phased arrays use multiple individual antenna elements to electronically steer the beam or create intentional signal voids known as nulls.


GPS/GNSS Antenna Fundamentals
GPS antennas must capture weak signals across specific frequency bands using right-hand circular polarization. Maintaining a low axial ratio and adequate gain at low elevation angles ensures the antenna can reliably track satellites near the horizon. Commercial aircraft standardly use FRPAs, which act as a baseline, single-element receiver with a fixed hemispherical pattern. CRPAs are multi-element arrays capable of suppressing interference by steering nulls directly toward jammers. Characterizing CRPAs requires testing to evaluate phase and amplitude matching between channels at both the element and array levels.


Measurement and Test Range Concepts
Benchtop RF measurements evaluate the fundamental properties of the antenna, capturing S-parameters and voltage standing wave ratio (VSWR) via a Vector Network Analyzer (VNA) to determine effective RF power delivery. To measure spatial properties without environmental interruption, testing occurs in an anechoic chamber, which uses RF-absorbing foam to eliminate multipath interference and reflections.


SDR and Positioner Integration
While a VNA provides high precision measurements, evaluating the null-steering of a CRPA requires multi-channel receivers. Software Defined Radios (SDRs) fulfill this role, acting as customizable signal sources and receivers that process RF data digitally. A mechanical positioner aligns the antenna in azimuth, elevation, and roll, sweeping it through specific angular steps to accurately map data to the physical orientation of the Device Under Test (DUT).

title: CRPA Antenna Characterization
text:
Methods

TP-Link Test Results
Before characterizing the provided GPS antennas, the team tested commercially available antennas such as the TP-Link. This provided a known reference against manufacturer datasheets to develop a testing methodology.
The TP-Link antenna was mounted inside the anechoic chamber and connected to a VNA. A calibrated horn antenna was used as the transmitting antenna. The VNA measured the transmission coefficient (\(S_{21}\)) between the transmitting and receiving antennas across a sweep of 2.1 GHz to 2.8 GHz. The antenna was rotated through a series of angular positions to collect gain data, which was processed in MATLAB to generate 2D radiation patterns.


Range & Calibration
All measurements were conducted in the 1x1x3 m³ anechoic chamber at Harvey Mudd College. The separation distance of 1.4 m ensured testing occurred in the far-field region.


SDR & Positioners
The HackRF One and the USRP x310 were used alongside GNU Radio to characterize the FRPA and CRPA. This allowed for customization of sampling rates, LNA gain, and bandwidth to conduct tests unattainable with just a VNA (e.g., null tests, SNR, beam steering).

title: CRPA Antenna Characterization
text:
Results

TP-Link Test Results
The first test measured the reflection coefficient in open air. We expected a decline in reflection coefficient at the transmitting frequencies of 2.4–2.5 GHz (at least -10dB return loss). At 2.4 GHz the return loss was about -20dB, and it remained under -10dB from 2.38 GHz–2.5 GHz, confirming proper VNA calibration.
The antenna gain was calculated using the Friis equation: \[ G_{rx} = P_{rx} - P_{tx} - G_{tx} - 20\log_{10}\left(\frac{\lambda}{4\pi d}\right) \] (Where \(G_{tx}\) is the calibration antenna gain, \(G_{rx}\) is the patch antenna gain, \(d\) is the distance between phase centers, and \(\lambda\) is the wavelength).
Using the Schwarzbeck calibration antenna (far-field gain of 12.49 dBi at 2.4 GHz) and a distance \(d = 1.45\) m, the measured peak gain initially read 6.3 dBi (short of the 9 dBi expected). After realigning the vertical phase centers and adjusting \(d\) to 1.4 m, we calculated a boresight gain of 8.34 dBi at 2.4 GHz, and a peak gain of 9.3 dBi at 2.475 GHz—successfully achieving the datasheet’s specification.


FRPA Results
The pattern was measured at 1.575 GHz (GPS L1 band). Initial manual trials showed a discontinuity at 270° broadside, likely due to human imprecision and strain on the SMA cable during 360-degree rotation. The datasheet pattern was measured with a circularly polarized signal, while our Schwarzbeck antenna is linearly polarized, resulting in a ~3dB power loss.
To investigate an unexpected rear lobe, we implemented a ground plane to block waves from reaching the far wall.


SDR Measurements vs. VNA
The first SDR trial showed a similar radiation pattern to the VNA manual measurements, retaining the 270° SMA cable strain anomaly. Future trials will implement cable strain relief and automated turntables to alleviate human positioning errors and optimize sweep times.

title: Labs
text:
Lab 1 - Board Assembly and Testing

Introduction
In this lab, the E155 board was assembled and tested it. After soldering all the components on, the FPGA was programmed to show hexadecimal digits on a 7 segment LED display. It takes four switches as binary inputs and outputs the corresponding hexadecimal digit. Additionally, an LED was blinked at 2.4 Hz using the ’s internal HSOSC and lowering it using a counter. To lower the HSOSC the following calculations were used. 48 MHz/ (2 * 10 MHz)


Design and Testing Methodology
The high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library was used to generate a clock signal at 24 MHz. A counter was then used to divide the clock signal down so the LED could blink at 2.4 Hz and make it easier to visualize. For the seven segment display, a case statement was used to assign all the inputs from the switches to the corresponding hexadecimal digit. The pins were carefully assigned from the FPGA to ensure they drove the intended section of the of seven segment display.
The design was developed using three modules. A top level module, a module for the counter, and a module for the seven segment display.
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository


Technical Documentation



Block Diagram


The block diagram in Figure 1 demonstrates the overall architecture of the design. The top level module includes three submodules: the the high-speed oscillator block (hf_osc), the counter module (blinking_led), and the seven segment display block (seven_segment_display).


Schematic



Schematic


The schematic in Figure 2 demonstrates the physical layout of the design. The LEDs from the seven segment display were connected to 150 Ω resistors. This was calculated using R = V/I. The voltage was found by subtracting the forward voltage of the LED from the power voltage and dividing by our desired current. (3.3V - 2.1 V) / 10 mA. This gave 120 Ω, so the standard resistor of 150 Ω was chosen.


Results and Discussion
All the prescribed tasks were accomplished. The seven segment display worked as expected, correctly shwoing the hexadecimal digits from 0 all the way to F. The LED blinked at 2.4 Hz showing it was designed correctly.


Testbench Simulation
The design met all intended design objectives.

Conclusion
The design successfully blinked an LED at 2.4 Hz and drove a seven segment LED display using switches as inputs. The intenral high-speed oscillator was used to generate the clock signal for the counter. I spent about 20 hours on this lab.


AI Prototype Summary
An LLM can be a helpful tool to write code. With a relatively short prompt, “Write SystemVerilog HDL to leverage the internal high speed oscillator in the Lattice UP5K FPGA and blink an LED at 2 Hz. Take full advantage of SystemVerilog syntax, for example, using logic instead of wire and reg.” The LLM was able to generate a file that was ready to be compiled. I tried to compile the file but ran into errors. I then had to paste the error messages a few more times before it was able to compile. I noticed that the AI was good about writing comments and describing what each code snippet should do. It wasn’t the best at writing code from scratch, and instead was more useful for debugging. It quickly caught syntax errors and identified issues when prompted. A useful way to levarage AI when making a design in Radiant is to use it as a debugging tool. It can explain error and warining messages and provide more context as to what Radiant is trying to tell you.

title: Esteban Gonzalez
text:
This lab used the skills acquired in labs 1 and 2. A system was designed to time multiplex a dual seven segment display to show 2 independent hexadecimal digit and those digits would be read from the presses of a keypad.



The design was developed to address the key bouncing that occurs on keyboards and still produce a desired output. My strategy to address the debouncing was first to send all the coloumn inputs through a synchronizer. This ensures there are no metastable values. When it receives an input, it enters a wait state. This just checks that p is the same value for the period. Once it passes that condition, it goes to a pressed state that outputs a 1, indicating that there has been a valid key pressed. Different types of FSMs were used. A FSM was used to address the bouncing of the physical keys and another FSM was used to control the display registers. These two FSMS were communicating in only one direction. The debounce module communicated to the key_press FSM to alert it when a key was pressed for a valid amount of time. I decided that they didn’t need to communicate between each other, as the debounce FSM can be updated straight from the coloumns of the keypad. The FSM is running all the time, and only changes states when it gets a signal from the keypad. For the purpose of this lab, that was fine as there were no power or hardware constraints.



The design was developed using eight modules. A top module, a counter module, a seven segment display module, a scanner module, a debounce module, a key press module, a synchronizer module, and a number assign module.

text:
This lab used the skills acquired in labs 1 and 2. A system was designed to time multiplex a dual seven segment display to show 2 independent hexadecimal digit and those digits would be read from the presses of a keypad.



The design was developed to address the key bouncing that occurs on keyboards and still produce a desired output. My strategy to address the debouncing was first to send all the coloumn inputs through a synchronizer. This ensures there are no metastable values. When it receives an input, it enters a wait state. This just checks that p is the same value for the period. Once it passes that condition, it goes to a pressed state that outputs a 1, indicating that there has been a valid key pressed. Different types of FSMs were used. A FSM was used to address the bouncing of the physical keys and another FSM was used to control the display registers. These two FSMS were communicating in only one direction. The debounce module communicated to the key_press FSM to alert it when a key was pressed for a valid amount of time. I decided that they didn’t need to communicate between each other, as the debounce FSM can be updated straight from the coloumns of the keypad. The FSM is running all the time, and only changes states when it gets a signal from the keypad. For the purpose of this lab, that was fine as there were no power or hardware constraints.



The design was developed using eight modules. A top module, a counter module, a seven segment display module, a scanner module, a debounce module, a key press module, a synchronizer module, and a number assign module.

title: Esteban Gonzalez
text:
In this lab, the STM32L432KC was used to read an encoder with two channels to determine the angular velocity of a brushed DC motor.



The design was developed using TIM2 and interrupts. Interrupts were used to accurately read the signals from the encoder at high speeds. A total of three header files were created to meet the design requirements.
The source code for the project can be found in the associated Github repository



The encoder has 2 channels that are 90 degrees out of phase with each other. As the motor spins, one channel goes high while the other stays low. Then as the motor continues spinning, the orignal channel goes low while the other goes high. This pattern generates a square wave that we can feed as an input into our microcontroller. The microcontroller then can read these square waves and calculate how many revoloutions the motor is doing. To find the revoloutions or angular velocity, the following calculations were used and implemented in software.
The angular velocity of the motor was calculated as follows:
First, we calculated the time between pulses and converted it to seconds
\(t = (current pulse - previous pulse)/1,000,000 us\)
Next, we need to calculate the frequency of the pulse in counts per second:
\(freq = (current count - previous count)/t\)
Lastly, we can calculate angular frequency revs/sec using the two values we already found:
\(angular velocity = freq/ t * 4*counts\)
where counts is the counts per revoloution of the motor. This value can be found from the motor datasheet. The reason we multiply by four is because in our code we look at the rising and falling edge of each encoder channel. The datasheet only reports the rising edge of one channel.
To verify the angular speed, an oscilliscope was used to measure the actual frequencies of the enncoder channels. Using the 12 V motor in the lab, the oscilliscope probe was connected to channel A. It was reading a frequency of 1.143 kHZ. We know the motor produces 408 pulses per revoloution, so plugging in these numbers into our calculations gives us:
\(angular velocity = (1.142 kHz)/ 408 pulses = 2.79 revs/sec\)
There is important things to consider when it comes to using interrupts versus polling at high speeds. In the case of the motor, that the encoder is constantly sending signals it is actually better to use polling instead of interrupts. The reason is that the motor speed can become fast enough that the pulse edges are arriving faster than the time it takes to process one ISR. This would make the main() code freeze, and the code we upload would effectively be trash. If you go the polling route, you can choose the sample rate which wouldn’t cause any negative effects in your code. For example, if the encoder was sending pulses at 4 MHz, an edge would arrive roughly once every 250 ns. This means the CPU has to read and update registers 4 million times per second. This also happens to be the speed the mcu clock is at, so it effectively jams the program. It won’t be able to execute code as it will be too busy handling the interrupts the entire time.power.






Schematic


The schematic in Figure 2 demonstrates the physical layout of the design. Pins 8 and 9 were connected to channels A and B of the encoder. This allowed the microcontroller to read the signals from the encoder and calculate the angular velocity.



Flowchart


The flowchart above represents the interrupts used for this lab.



All the prescribed tasks were accomplished successfully. The microcontroller was able to accurately read the revoultions per second of the motor. Even at full speed or extremely low speed, the microcontroller was still able to report sensible values for angular velocity.



After plugging in “Write me interrupt handlers to interface with a quadrature encoder. I’m using the STM32L432KC, what pins should I connect the encoder to in order to allow it to easily trigger the interrupts?” to gemini, it gave me surprisingly good recommendations. It recommended pins PA0 and PA1 which map directly to TIM2. Outside of that, the output of gemini was not the best. It provided a lot of extra things that were not neccessary, such as an error counter and a “Hardware input filter to suppress bounce noise”. I believe the encoders don’t have bounce noise as they are not buttons.
